blocks.text: A modern gas-turbine power station converts only about 38 per cent of its fuel energy into electricity, yet its exhaust leaves the turbine near 600 °C and still carries almost two thirds of the fuel energy. Pass that exhaust through a steam boiler and a steam turbine, and the same fuel produces electricity at 55 to 60 per cent efficiency. That is the combined cycle, the most efficient thermal power plant in routine operation.

blocks.markdown: The **Brayton cycle** is the ideal model of a gas turbine. Air is compressed (1→2), heated at constant pressure by burning fuel (2→3), expanded through a turbine (3→4) and exhausted. For analysis we use the **cold-air-standard** assumptions: the working fluid is air as an ideal gas with constant $c_p=1.005$ kJ/(kg K) and ratio of specific heats $k=1.4$ (typical), and the heat addition replaces combustion. With a pressure ratio $r_p=p_2/p_1$, the exponent $(k-1)/k=0.2857$ appears in every temperature relation.

blocks.title: Isentropic efficiencies of compressor and turbine
blocks.text: The compressor needs more work than the isentropic value: $\eta_c=(T_{2s}-T_1)/(T_2-T_1)$. The turbine delivers less: $\eta_t=(T_3-T_4)/(T_3-T_{4s})$. The isentropic outlet temperatures are $T_{2s}=T_1r_p^{(k-1)/k}$ and $T_{4s}=T_3/r_p^{(k-1)/k}$. Because a gas turbine's compressor absorbs a large fraction of the turbine's output (the **back-work ratio** $w_c/w_t$, typically 0.4 to 0.6), compressor and turbine irreversibility cut net work sharply.

blocks.caption: Net work, heat input and thermal efficiency of a Brayton cycle; the ideal efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio

blocks.title: Brayton cycle with real components
blocks.prompt: Air enters at 300 K. The pressure ratio is 10 and the turbine inlet temperature is 1300 K. Compressor and turbine isentropic efficiencies are 0.85 and 0.88. Take $c_p=1.005$ kJ/(kg K), $k=1.4$. Find the net work, thermal efficiency and back-work ratio.

steps.text: Isentropic and real compressor outlet temperatures.
Isentropic and real turbine outlet temperatures.

blocks.answer: Net work is about 224 kJ/kg and the thermal efficiency about 0.332 (against 0.482 ideal). The compressor takes about 59.6% of the turbine work.

blocks.caption: Effect of pressure ratio at $T_1=300$ K and $T_3=1300$ K

blocks.markdown: **Effect of pressure ratio.** For the ideal cycle the efficiency $1-r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$ rises steadily with pressure ratio. The **specific work**, however, has a maximum: at very low $r_p$ there is little expansion, and at very high $r_p$ the compressor outlet temperature approaches $T_3$, leaving little heat to add. For the ideal cycle the work peaks at $r_p=(T_3/T_1)^{k/[2(k-1)]}$. With real components the efficiency also peaks, at a pressure ratio well below the ideal value, as the table shows, because compressor and turbine losses grow with the pressure ratio and $T_2$ approaches $T_3$.

blocks.caption: Pressure ratio for maximum specific work of the ideal cycle, and the combined-cycle efficiency (epsilon is the fraction of exhaust heat recovered)

blocks.title: Combined-cycle efficiency
blocks.prompt: A gas turbine (topping cycle) has thermal efficiency 0.36. Its exhaust heat, the fraction $(1-\eta_g)$ of the fuel energy, passes to a heat-recovery steam generator and then a steam cycle (bottoming cycle) with efficiency 0.33 on the heat it receives. Find the overall efficiency (a) if all the exhaust heat is recovered and (b) if only 85% is recovered.

steps.text: Exhaust heat per unit of fuel energy.
Case (a): full recovery. The steam cycle turns this heat into work with efficiency $\eta_s$.

blocks.answer: Overall efficiency is about 0.571 for full recovery and about 0.54 with 85% recovery, both well above the gas turbine alone.

items: Find $T_{2s}$ and $T_2$ from the pressure ratio and compressor efficiency; find $T_{4s}$ and $T_4$ from the turbine efficiency.
Net work is turbine work minus compressor work; heat input is $c_p(T_3-T_2)$.
For pressure-ratio studies, compare the ideal and real cycles at several $r_p$; specific work peaks at an intermediate value.
For a combined cycle, treat the exhaust as the heat source of the bottoming cycle and apply $\eta_{cc}=\eta_g+\varepsilon(1-\eta_g)\eta_s$.

blocks.title: Why the combined cycle works
blocks.text: The gas turbine rejects its heat at a high temperature (several hundred °C), so a steam cycle can use that heat before it is wasted. The topping cycle adds heat at a very high temperature and the bottoming cycle rejects heat at ambient temperature, so the overall cycle approaches a larger temperature difference. The overall efficiency is limited by the second law to below $1-T_L/T_H$, where $T_H$ is the turbine inlet temperature.

points: Brayton cycle: $w_{net}=c_p[(T_3-T_4)-(T_2-T_1)]$, with real components using $\eta_c$ and $\eta_t$; the back-work ratio is large.
Ideal efficiency $1-r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$ rises with pressure ratio; specific work peaks at an intermediate ratio and real efficiency also peaks.
Combined cycle: $\eta_{cc}=\eta_g+\varepsilon(1-\eta_g)\eta_s$, much higher than either cycle alone.

questions.stem: A gas turbine's compressor absorbs 380 kJ/kg and its turbine produces 640 kJ/kg. The back-work ratio and the net work are respectively:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ratio of compressor work to turbine work, and their difference.
distractorRationale.b: Inverts the ratio of the works.
distractorRationale.c: Adds the works instead of subtracting.
distractorRationale.d: Uses the ratio of net work to turbine work, the complement of the back-work ratio.

questions.explanation: The back-work ratio is $w_c/w_t=380/640=0.594$, so the compressor uses about 59 per cent of the turbine work. The net work is $640-380=260$ kJ/kg.

questions.stem: The compressor isentropic efficiency of a gas turbine falls because of fouling, with the same pressure ratio and turbine inlet temperature. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The compressor work falls, so the net work rises
The compressor work rises, so the net work and thermal efficiency both fall
The compressor work rises, but the net work is unchanged because the turbine compensates
The compressor outlet temperature falls, so less heat must be added and the efficiency rises

questions.correctOptionText: The compressor work rises, so the net work and thermal efficiency both fall

distractorRationale.a: A lower efficiency means more work is needed for the same pressure ratio.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: more compressor work means less net work and lower efficiency.
distractorRationale.c: The turbine work does not rise; the net work falls.
distractorRationale.d: The real outlet temperature rises with irreversibility, although heat input falls slightly; the net work falls by more.

questions.explanation: The real work $c_p(T_2-T_1)=c_p(T_{2s}-T_1)/\eta_c$ increases as $\eta_c$ decreases. The turbine work is unchanged, so $w_{net}$ falls; heat input falls only slightly because $T_2$ is higher, so efficiency also falls.

questions.stem: In the ideal cold-air-standard Brayton cycle, what determines the thermal efficiency?

options.text: Only the pressure ratio (for a given ratio of specific heats): $\eta=1-r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$
The mass flow rate of air

questions.correctOptionText: Only the pressure ratio (for a given ratio of specific heats): $\eta=1-r_p^{-(k-1)/k}$

distractorRationale.a: The ideal efficiency is independent of $T_3$; $T_3$ affects the specific work.
distractorRationale.b: The temperature ratios cancel, so $T_1$ does not appear.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it depends on pressure ratio and k alone.
distractorRationale.d: The mass flow sets the power but not the efficiency.

questions.explanation: The ideal heat added and rejected both scale with the same temperature ratio, which equals $r_p^{(k-1)/k}$, so the efficiency depends only on $r_p$ and $k$. Raising the turbine inlet temperature raises the work per kg but not the ideal efficiency.

questions.stem: An ideal Brayton cycle has a ratio of maximum to minimum temperature $T_3/T_1=4.0$ ($k=1.4$). The pressure ratio that gives the maximum specific net work is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Equates the pressure ratio to the temperature ratio, which is incorrect.
distractorRationale.b: Uses the exponent k/(k-1) without the factor of a half, which is the exponent for the temperature-pressure relation, not the work maximum.
distractorRationale.c: Uses k/2 as the exponent, which has no basis in the optimisation.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the temperature ratio raised to k over 2(k minus 1).

questions.explanation: For the ideal cycle, the net work peaks at $r_p=(T_3/T_1)^{k/[2(k-1)]}=4^{1.75}=11.31$. At lower pressure ratios the expansion is too small; at higher ratios the compressor takes too large a share.

questions.stem: A gas turbine of efficiency 0.34 exhausts to a heat-recovery steam generator that recovers all of the exhaust heat for a steam cycle of efficiency 0.30. The combined-cycle efficiency is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: topping efficiency plus bottoming efficiency applied to the rejected fraction.
distractorRationale.b: Adds the efficiencies, double counting the fuel energy.
distractorRationale.c: Multiplies the efficiencies, which applies to cycles in series on the same heat, not to a topping and bottoming arrangement.
distractorRationale.d: Averages the two efficiencies, ignoring that the steam cycle uses heat the gas turbine rejected.

questions.explanation: The gas turbine converts 0.34 of the fuel energy to work and rejects 0.66. The steam cycle converts 0.30 of that: $0.66\times0.30=0.198$. The total is $0.34+0.198=0.538$.

questions.stem: A gas turbine takes in air at 290 K, with a pressure ratio of 8 and a turbine inlet temperature of 1250 K. The compressor isentropic efficiency is 0.82 and that of the turbine 0.87. Using $c_p=1.005$ kJ/(kg K) and $k=1.4$ for the air throughout, find the net specific work in kJ/kg.
An ideal air-standard Brayton cycle with $k=1.4$ operates at a pressure ratio of 14. Find its thermal efficiency as a fraction.
questions.explanation: $\eta=1-r_p^{-(k-1)/k}=1-14^{-0.2857}=1-0.4705=0.5295$. The real cycle with component losses would have a markedly lower efficiency.

questions.stem: A gas turbine of efficiency 0.38 has its exhaust heat passed to a steam bottoming cycle of efficiency 0.35 on the heat it receives, through a heat-recovery steam generator that captures 80% of the exhaust heat. Find the overall combined-cycle efficiency as a fraction.
questions.explanation: The exhaust heat is $1-0.38=0.62$ of the fuel energy; 80% of it is recovered, i.e. $0.80\times0.62=0.496$, and the steam cycle makes work $0.35\times0.496=0.1736$. Adding the gas-turbine output gives $0.38+0.1736=0.5536$.

questions.stem: Explain why the net specific work of a Brayton cycle has a maximum at an intermediate pressure ratio, and why a real cycle's thermal efficiency peaks at a moderate pressure ratio even though the ideal cycle's efficiency keeps rising. State how a higher turbine inlet temperature changes the optimum.
markingGuide: Ideal efficiency = 1 - r_p^(-(k-1)/k) rises monotonically with r_p
Specific work: at low r_p expansion small, at very high r_p compressor outlet temperature approaches T3 so net work falls to zero; maximum at r_p = (T3/T1)^(k/(2(k-1))) for the ideal cycle
Real components: compressor work grows and turbine expansion shrinks in relative terms with r_p, and irreversibility scales with the work; losses increase with r_p
Back-work ratio increases with r_p so net work falls from a peak at a lower r_p than ideal and efficiency peaks
A higher T3 raises the specific work and moves the optimum r_p higher
Practical implication: pick r_p between that for max work and max efficiency
questions.explanation: In the ideal cycle, work is zero at both extremes of pressure ratio so it peaks in between. Real losses are proportional to the work done by each component, so as the pressure ratio rises, the compressor absorbs an increasing share of turbine work and the real efficiency eventually falls. Raising $T_3$ increases the available expansion work and moves the optimum to a higher pressure ratio.

questions.stem: Describe how a combined-cycle plant uses a gas turbine and a steam cycle together. Derive the overall efficiency in terms of the topping efficiency $\eta_g$, the bottoming efficiency $\eta_s$ and the recovery fraction $\varepsilon$, and explain why the result cannot exceed the Carnot limit.
markingGuide: Gas turbine exhaust heat feeds a heat-recovery steam generator that raises steam for the bottoming (Rankine) cycle
Energy: fuel energy Q_f; gas turbine work = eta_g Q_f; exhaust heat (1 - eta_g) Q_f available
Recovered heat = epsilon (1 - eta_g) Q_f gives steam work eta_s epsilon (1 - eta_g) Q_f
Overall eta_cc = eta_g + epsilon (1 - eta_g) eta_s (or eta_g + eta_s - eta_g eta_s for epsilon = 1)
Exceeds both individual efficiencies because the rejected heat of the top cycle is reused
The efficiency still stays below the Carnot limit 1 - T_L/T_H, with T_H the turbine inlet temperature and T_L ambient, as the combined plant takes heat at T_H and rejects at about ambient
questions.explanation: Applying the first law to the fuel energy gives the sum of the gas-turbine work and the steam-turbine work obtained from the recovered exhaust heat. Because the heat is added at very high temperature and finally rejected near ambient temperature, the combined cycle approaches, but cannot reach, the Carnot efficiency for those temperatures.
